claim: Progression through mitosis is driven by a protein phosphorylation wave that depends on an activation-inactivation cycle of cyclin B-dependent kinase (Cdk) 1.
source: During cell division, progression through mitosis is driven by a protein phosphorylation wave. This wave namely depends on an activation-inactivation cycle of cyclin B-dependent kinase (Cdk) 1
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about cell cycle regulation and is presented as background information.

claim: Activities of major protein phosphatases like PP1 and PP2A appear directly or indirectly repressed by Cdk1.
source: while activities of major protein phosphatases, like PP1 and PP2A, appear directly or indirectly repressed by Cdk1
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about phosphatase regulation during mitosis.

claim: Activation of PP2A-B55 required the phosphatase Fcp1 downstream of Cdk1 inactivation in human cells.
source: We show here that activation of PP2A-B55, a major mitosis exit phosphatase, required the phosphatase Fcp1 downstream Cdk1 inactivation in human cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in the manuscript.

claim: During mitosis exit, Fcp1 bound Greatwall (Gwl).
source: During mitosis exit, Fcp1 bound Greatwall (Gwl)
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Fcp1 dephosphorylated Gwl at Cdk1 phosphorylation sites during mitosis exit.
source: During mitosis exit, Fcp1 bound Greatwall (Gwl), a Cdk1-stimulated kinase that phosphorylates Ensa/ARPP19 and converts these proteins into potent PP2A-B55 inhibitors during mitosis onset, and dephosphorylated it at Cdk1 phosphorylation sites.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing Fcp1-dependent dephosphorylation of Gwl at S90 and S453 sites.

claim: Gwl is a Cdk1-stimulated kinase that phosphorylates Ensa/ARPP19 and converts these proteins into potent PP2A-B55 inhibitors during mitosis onset.
source: Greatwall (Gwl), a Cdk1-stimulated kinase that phosphorylates Ensa/ARPP19 and converts these proteins into potent PP2A-B55 inhibitors during mitosis onset
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: Fcp1-catalyzed dephosphorylation drastically reduced Gwl kinase activity towards Ensa/ARPP19.
source: Fcp1-catalyzed dephosphorylation drastically reduced Gwl kinase activity towards Ensa/ARPP19 promoting PP2A-B55 activation.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro kinase assays shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Fcp1-catalyzed dephosphorylation of Gwl promotes PP2A-B55 activation.
source: Fcp1-catalyzed dephosphorylation drastically reduced Gwl kinase activity towards Ensa/ARPP19 promoting PP2A-B55 activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that Fcp1 reduces Gwl activity, which would relieve PP2A-B55 inhibition.

claim: Fcp1 coordinates Cdk1 and Gwl inactivation to derepress PP2A-B55, generating a dephosphorylation switch that drives mitosis progression.
source: Thus, Fcp1 coordinates Cdk1 and Gwl inactivation to derepress PP2A-B55, generating a dephosphorylation switch that drives mitosis progression.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Fcp1 has a critical, transcription-independent role in Cdk1 inactivation at the end of mitosis.
source: We recently reported a critical, transcription-independent, role for the essential RNA polymerase II-carboxy-terminal domain (RNAP II-CTD) phosphatase Fcp1 in Cdk1 inactivation at the end of mitosis (Visconti et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Depleting Fcp1 from living HeLa cells substantially impaired cyclin B degradation, Cdk1 inactivation and mitosis exit.
source: Indeed, depleting Fcp1 from living HeLa cells as well as from mitotic HeLa cell extracts, that are nuclei-free thus non-transcribing, substantially impaired cyclin B degradation, Cdk1 inactivation and mitosis exit (Visconti et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Depleting Fcp1 from mitotic HeLa cell extracts substantially impaired cyclin B degradation, Cdk1 inactivation and mitosis exit.
source: Indeed, depleting Fcp1 from living HeLa cells as well as from mitotic HeLa cell extracts, that are nuclei-free thus non-transcribing, substantially impaired cyclin B degradation, Cdk1 inactivation and mitosis exit (Visconti et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Mitotic HeLa cell extracts are nuclei-free and thus non-transcribing.
source: from mitotic HeLa cell extracts, that are nuclei-free thus non-transcribing
evidence: This is a methodological fact about the experimental system used.

claim: Fcp1 depletion impaired bulk mitotic protein dephosphorylation upon chemical inhibition of Cdk1 in non-transcribing mitotic cell extracts.
source: In that study, we also noticed that Fcp1 depletion impaired bulk mitotic protein dephosphorylation also upon chemical inhibition of Cdk1 in non-transcribing mitotic cell extracts (Visconti et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Fcp1 is required for crucial mitosis exit dephosphorylations even downstream of Cdk1 inactivation in a transcription-independent manner.
source: This observation suggested that Fcp1 was required for crucial mitosis exit dephosphorylations even downstream Cdk1 inactivation in a transcription-independent manner.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Fcp1 depletion impairs dephosphorylation even when Cdk1 is chemically inhibited.

claim: Bulk dephosphorylation at mitosis exit are likely due to action of major phosphatases like PP1 or PP2A, rather than Fcp1 itself.
source: However, bulk dephosphorylation at mitosis exit are likely due to action of major phosphatases like PP1 or PP2A, rather than Fcp1 itself (Ferrigno et al., 1993; Qian et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PP2A-B55 has relevant roles for late mitotic events like spindle breakdown, chromatin decondensation, nuclear membrane and Golgi reassembly and cytokinesis.
source: The PP2A-B55 isoform, in particular, has relevant roles for late mitotic events like spindle breakdown, chromatin decondensation, nuclear membrane and Golgi reassembly and cytokinesis (Schmitz et al., 2010; Cundell et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PP2A-B55 reverses bulk mitotic phosphorylations detectable by anti-Cdk1 substrate antibody recognizing the K/HpSP motif.
source: In addition, PP2A-B55 has been shown to reverse bulk mitotic phosphorylations detectable by a commercially available anti-Cdk1 substrate antibody, recognizing the K/HpSP motif (where pS is phosphorylated Ser), and the phosphorylation of PRC1, a crucial cytokinesis protein, at T481 (Schmitz et al., 2010; Cundell et al., 2013; Qian et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PP2A-B55 reverses the phosphorylation of PRC1 at T481.
source: In addition, PP2A-B55 has been shown to reverse bulk mitotic phosphorylations detectable by a commercially available anti-Cdk1 substrate antibody, recognizing the K/HpSP motif (where pS is phosphorylated Ser), and the phosphorylation of PRC1, a crucial cytokinesis protein, at T481 (Schmitz et al., 2010; Cundell et al., 2013; Qian et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PRC1 is a crucial cytokinesis protein.
source: and the phosphorylation of PRC1, a crucial cytokinesis protein, at T481
evidence: This is established knowledge about PRC1 function.

claim: Dephosphorylations of bulk K/HpSP motif and pT481-PRC1 at mitosis exit are dependent on Fcp1.
source: In preliminary experiments, in which Fcp1 expression was downregulated in HeLa cells by small interfering RNAs (siRNAs), we found that dephosphorylations of bulk K/HpSP motif and pT481-PRC1 at mitosis exit were indeed dependent on Fcp1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Fcp1 depletion impaired bulk K/HpSP motif and pT481-PRC1 dephosphorylation upon chemical inhibition of Cdk1 activity in mitotic cells.
source: To know whether Fcp1 controlled PP2A-B55 activation downstream Cdk1 inactivation, we determined whether Fcp1 depletion impaired bulk K/HpSP motif and pT481-PRC1 dephosphorylation upon chemical inhibition of Cdk1 activity in mitotic cells and cell extracts.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,C.

claim: Fcp1 depletion impaired bulk K/HpSP motif and pT481-PRC1 dephosphorylation upon chemical inhibition of Cdk1 activity in mitotic cell extracts.
source: To know whether Fcp1 controlled PP2A-B55 activation downstream Cdk1 inactivation, we determined whether Fcp1 depletion impaired bulk K/HpSP motif and pT481-PRC1 dephosphorylation upon chemical inhibition of Cdk1 activity in mitotic cells and cell extracts.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,C.

claim: In cells and cell extracts, Fcp1 is required for timely PP2A-B55-dependent dephosphorylations following Cdk1 inactivation.
source: The results showed that, in cells and cell extracts, Fcp1 was indeed required for timely PP2A-B55-dependent dephosphorylations following Cdk1 inactivation (Figure 1A,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,C.

claim: Fcp1 is relatively resistant to the potent PP2A inhibitor okadaic acid (OA).
source: Fcp1 is relatively resistant to the potent PP2A inhibitor okadaic acid (OA)
evidence: This is established knowledge about Fcp1 biochemical properties.

claim: pT481-PRC1 and bulk K/HpSP motif dephosphorylations are okadaic acid sensitive.
source: nevertheless, we confirmed that pT481-PRC1 and bulk K/HpSP motif dephosphorylations were OA sensitive (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) (Schmitz et al., 2010; Cundell et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and citations.

claim: PP2A-B55 activation might require Fcp1 downstream of Cdk1 inactivation.
source: Considering that pT481-PRC1 and bulk K/HpSP motif dephosphorylations at mitosis exit have been shown to depend on PP2A-B55 activity (Schmitz et al., 2010; Cundell et al., 2013), together, our data suggested that PP2A-B55 activation might require Fcp1 downstream Cdk1 inactivation.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and cited literature.

claim: In Fcp1-depleted cells, PRC1 poorly concentrated at spindle midzone, even upon Cdk1 inhibition.
source: Nevertheless, we found that in Fcp1-depleted cells PRC1 poorly concentrated at spindle midzone, even upon Cdk1 inhibition (Figure 1—figure supplements 3A,3B)
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 3A,3B.

claim: Fcp1 depletion induced accumulation of binucleated cells in asynchronously growing cells.
source: and that Fcp1 depletion induced several mitotic phenotypes in asynchronously growing cells, in addition to cell death, including accumulation of binucleated cells, suggesting that Fcp1 was indeed required also for proficient cytokinesis (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Fcp1 depletion induced cell death in asynchronously growing cells.
source: and that Fcp1 depletion induced several mitotic phenotypes in asynchronously growing cells, in addition to cell death
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Fcp1 is required for proficient cytokinesis.
source: suggesting that Fcp1 was indeed required also for proficient cytokinesis (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of binucleated cells upon Fcp1 depletion.

claim: During mitosis onset, PP2A-B55 is inhibited by Cdk1 phosphorylating and stimulating Gwl kinase that represses PP2A-B55 activity by phosphorylating Ensa/ARPP19.
source: During mitosis onset, PP2A-B55 is inhibited by a recently elucidated pathway: Cdk1 phosphorylates and stimulates Gwl kinase that, in turn, represses PP2A-B55 activity by phosphorylating Ensa/ARPP19 and converting these proteins into potent PP2A-B55 inhibitors (Schmitz et al., 2010; Castilho et al., 2009; Vigneron et al. 2009; Lorca and Castro, 2013; Mochida and Hunt, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: How the PP2A-B55 inhibition condition is reversed at the end of mitosis is still unclear.
source: How this condition is reversed at the end of mitosis is still unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The Fcp1 phosphatase has been called in the mechanism for PP2A-B55 reactivation at mitosis exit.
source: The Fcp1 phosphatase has already been called in the mechanism for PP2A-B55 reactivation at mitosis exit (Hegarat et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Fcp1-depleted mitotic cells maintain Gwl-dependent phosphorylation of Ensa at S67 upon Cdk1 inhibition.
source: Indeed, Fcp1-depleted, mitotic cells were found to maintain Gwl-dependent phosphorylation of Ensa (at S67 in human Ensa; pS67-Ensa) upon Cdk1 inhibition, and some evidence was provided that Fcp1 directly dephosphorylated pS67-Ensa to allow PP2A-B55 reactivation (Hegarat et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Evidence was provided that Fcp1 directly dephosphorylated pS67-Ensa to allow PP2A-B55 reactivation.
source: and some evidence was provided that Fcp1 directly dephosphorylated pS67-Ensa to allow PP2A-B55 reactivation (Hegarat et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work, though the authors later challenge this conclusion.

claim: PP2A-B55 itself, rather than Fcp1, dephosphorylates pS67-Ensa and autoactivates.
source: However, this evidence was subsequently challenged by Williams and co-workers who showed that PP2A-B55 itself, rather than Fcp1, dephosphorylated pS67-Ensa and autoactivated, although this slow reaction could be rapidly reversed as long as Gwl stays active (Williams et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: PP2A-B55 autoactivation is a slow reaction that can be rapidly reversed as long as Gwl stays active.
source: PP2A-B55 itself, rather than Fcp1, dephosphorylated pS67-Ensa and autoactivated, although this slow reaction could be rapidly reversed as long as Gwl stays active (Williams et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Fcp1 is unable to specifically dephosphorylate pS67-Ensa in vitro.
source: We tested the ability of Fcp1 to dephosphorylate specifically pS67-Ensa in vitro and found that, in agreement with Williams and coworkers conclusions (Williams et al., 2014), Fcp1 was unable to do so (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Gwl is highly phosphorylated in mitosis.
source: Gwl is higly phosphorylated in mitosis
evidence: This is established knowledge about Gwl regulation.

claim: Cdk1 directly phosphorylates Gwl stimulating its kinase activity.
source: and several observations indicate that Cdk1 directly phosphorylates Gwl stimulating its kinase activity (Vigneron et al., 2011; Blake-Hodek et al., 2012; Dephoure et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Once activated by Cdk1, Gwl can autophosphorylate.
source: Once activated by Cdk1, Gwl can autophosphorylate
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Gwl autophosphorylation contributes to its own overall activity.
source: and autophosphorylation appears to contribute to its own overall activity (Blake-Hodek et al. 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: PP1 is the phosphatase that dephosphorylates Gwl at autophosphorylation sites, contributing to Gwl inactivation at the end of mitosis.
source: A study in Xenopus laevis egg extracts has very recently provided compelling evidence that PP1 is the phosphatase that dephosphorylates Gwl at autophosphorylation sites, contributing this way to Gwl inactivation at the end of mitosis.
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent research.

claim: Dephosphorylation of Gwl at sites other than autophosphorylation sites, most likely those phosphorylated by Cdk1, is PP1-independent.
source: However, the same study showed that dephosphorylation of Gwl at other sites, most likely also those phosphorylated by Cdk1, is PP1-independent (Heim et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent research.

claim: Fcp1 is able to reverse Cdk-dependent phosphorylation.
source: As Fcp1 is known to be able to reverse Cdk-dependent phosphorylation (Ghosh et al., 2008; Visconti et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Serine 90 and serine 453 in human Gwl are the only human Gwl serine residues in K/HpSP and pSPXR/K contexts, respectively.
source: Two commercially available anti-Cdk1 substrate antibodies, the previously mentioned anti-K/HpSP motif and an anti-pSPXR/K (where pS is phosphorylated serine and X any aminoacid) motif, can in principle recognize serine 90 and serine 453 in human Gwl (S90-Gwl and S453-Gwl), respectively, being S90-Gwl (89-KSP-91) and S453-Gwl (453-SPCK-456), the only human Gwl serine residues in those contexts.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of human Gwl.

claim: S453-Gwl has been shown to be specifically phosphorylated in mitosis by proteomic approaches.
source: While S453-Gwl has been shown to be specifically phosphorylated in mitosis by proteomic approaches, S90-Gwl has not (Dephoure et al., 2008; Blake-Hodek et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous proteomic studies.

claim: S90-Gwl has not been shown to be specifically phosphorylated in mitosis by proteomic approaches.
source: While S453-Gwl has been shown to be specifically phosphorylated in mitosis by proteomic approaches, S90-Gwl has not (Dephoure et al., 2008; Blake-Hodek et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous proteomic studies.

claim: Anti-K/HpSP and anti-pSPXR/K antibodies react against V5-tagged wild-type Gwl but not against V5-Gwl versions in which serine 90 and serine 453 were mutated to alanine when isolated from transfected, mitotic, HeLa cells.
source: Nevertheless, both antibodies reacted against V5-tagged wild-type Gwl (V5-GwlWT) but not against V5-Gwl versions in which serine 90 and serine 453 were respectively mutated into non-phosphorylatable alanine (V5-GwlS90A; V5-GwlS453A) when the tagged proteins were isolated from transfected, mitotic, HeLa cells, indicating that both residues are phosphorylated in mitosis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Both S90 and S453 residues of Gwl are phosphorylated in mitosis.
source: indicating that both residues are phosphorylated in mitosis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is inferred from the antibody reactivity data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Anti-K/HpSP and anti-pSPXR/K antibodies do not react against V5-GwlWT isolated from HeLa cells in G1, unless it is treated with purified, active, Cdk1 in vitro.
source: In addition, these antibodies did not react against V5-GwlWT isolated from HeLa cells in G1, unless it was treated with purified, active, Cdk1 in vitro (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: pS90- and pS453-Gwl signals were readily detected in prometaphase but were progressively lost as cells transited out of mitosis.
source: PS90- and pS453-Gwl signals were readly detected in prometaphase but were progressively lost as cells transited out of mitosis (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Dephosphorylation of Gwl at S90 and S453 was resistant to okadaic acid at 2 μM.
source: Importantly, dephosphorylation at both sites was resistant to OA at a dose (2 μM) that potently inhibited PP1 (Figure 2C)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: 2 μM okadaic acid potently inhibits PP1.
source: dephosphorylation at both sites was resistant to OA at a dose (2 μM) that potently inhibited PP1 (Figure 2C), as indicated by persistance, despite Cdk1 inactivation by cyclin B degradation, of Cdk1-dependent inhibitory phosphorylation of PP1 catalytic subunit a (PP1cα) at T320 (pT320-PP1cα), a site that PP1 autodephosphorylates upon Cdk1 inactivation (Qian et al., 2013; Heim et al., 2015) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is inferred from the persistence of pT320-PP1cα in the presence of OA.

claim: PP1 autodephosphorylates T320 of PP1cα upon Cdk1 inactivation.
source: a site that PP1 autodephosphorylates upon Cdk1 inactivation (Qian et al., 2013; Heim et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Okadaic acid significantly delayed the kinetics of Gwl migration shift on SDS/PAGE.
source: However, OA significantly delayed the kinetics of Gwl migration shift on SDS/PAGE, in agreement with the notion that also OA-sensitive phosphatase(s) dephosphorylate Gwl at several other sites during mitosis exit (Hegarat et al., 2014; Williams et al., 2014; Heim et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observation and citations.

claim: OA-sensitive phosphatase(s) dephosphorylate Gwl at several other sites during mitosis exit.
source: in agreement with the notion that also OA-sensitive phosphatase(s) dephosphorylate Gwl at several other sites during mitosis exit (Hegarat et al., 2014; Williams et al., 2014; Heim et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Depletion of Fcp1 delayed Gwl dephosphorylation at both S90 and S453 as well as Gwl migration shift and pS67-Ensa dephosphorylation.
source: Conversely, depletion of Fcp1 delayed Gwl dephosphorylation at both S90 and S453 as well as Gwl migration shift and pS67-Ensa dephosphorylation (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: A 15-min treatment with RO-3306 promptly induced pS90- and pS453-Gwl dephosphorylation and Gwl downshift in prometaphase-arrested control and Fcp1 re-expressing cells but not in prometaphase-arrested Fcp1-depleted cells.
source: In addition, a 15-min treatment with RO-3306 promptly induced pS90- and pS453-Gwl dephosphorylation and Gwl downshift in prometaphase-arrested control and Fcp1 re-expressing cells but not in prometaphase-arrested Fcp1-depleted cells, indicating that Fcp1 was required for these dephosphorylations downstream Cdk1 inactivation (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Fcp1 is required for pS90- and pS453-Gwl dephosphorylation downstream of Cdk1 inactivation.
source: indicating that Fcp1 was required for these dephosphorylations downstream Cdk1 inactivation (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Prolonging Cdk1 inhibitor treatment up to 30 min resulted in some Gwl dephosphorylation also in Fcp1 siRNAs-treated cells.
source: Prolonging Cdk1 inhibitor treatment up to 30 min resulted in some Gwl dephosphorylation also in Fcp1 siRNAs-treated cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The 15-min treatment with RO-3306 was able to potently induce autoactivatory pT320-PP1cα dephosphorylation in Fcp1-depleted as in control cells.
source: Nevertheless, the 15-min treatment with RO-3306 was able to potently induce autoactivatory pT320-PP1cα dephosphorylation in Fcp1-depleted as in control cells (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Fcp1 is required for timely dephosphorylation of at least two Cdk1-dependent sites of Gwl, S90 and S453, at mitosis exit.
source: Thus, Fcp1 is required for timely dephosphorylation of at least two Cdk1-dependent sites of Gwl, S90 and S453, at mitosis exit.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Fcp1 can be found in complexes with its substrates.
source: As Fcp1 can be found in complexes with its substrates (Visconti et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Gwl transiently bound Fcp1 during mitosis exit.
source: Indeed, by co-immunoprecipitation (coIP) of endogenous proteins, we found that Gwl transiently bound Fcp1 during mitosis exit (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Gwl-Fcp1 binding was lower in prometaphase, increased during the period of spindle assembly (20-30 min) to decrease thereafter.
source: Binding was lower in prometaphase, increased during the period of spindle assembly (20-30 min) to decrease thereafter (Figure 3A
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Approximately 8-14% of Fcp1 interacts with Gwl in cells at the peak of interaction.
source: Fcp1 and Gwl appear to be similarly abundant proteins in HeLa cells and we estimate that approximately 8-14% of Fcp1 interacts with Gwl in cells at the peak of interaction as, routinely, ~3-5% of total lysate Fcp1 was found in Gwl IP that contained ~30-40% of total lysate Gwl
evidence: This is estimated from quantitative analysis of immunoprecipitation data.

claim: In Fcp1-depleted cells complemented with exogenous Fcp1, Gwl interacted with the exogenous protein with similar kinetics observed with the endogenous Fcp1.
source: In Fcp1-depleted cells complemented with exogenous Fcp1, Gwl interacted with the exogenous protein with similar kinetics observed with the endogenous Fcp1 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Transient Gwl-Fcp1 interaction was detected during mitosis exit in non-transformed, telomerase-immortalized, human retinal pigment epithelium cells hTERT-RPE1.
source: Transient Gwl-Fcp1 interaction was also detected during mitosis exit in non-transformed, telomerase-immortalized, human retinal pigment epithelium cells hTERT-RPE1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Fcp1 bound and dephosphorylated Gwl at S90 and S453, and possibly at other Cdk1-dependent sites, during mitosis exit.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that Fcp1 bound and dephosphorylated Gwl at S90 and S453, and possibly at other Cdk1-dependent sites, during mitosis exit
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Fcp1-catalyzed dephosphorylation lowered Gwl activity towards Ensa/ARPP19, allowing PP2A-B55 to autoactivate.
source: and that Fcp1-catalyzed dephosphorylation lowered Gwl activity towards Ensa/ARPP19, allowing PP2A-B55 to autoactivate.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Purified active Fcp1 (Fcp1WT), but not an inactive, catalytic dead, Fcp1 version (Fcp1CD), dephosphorylated Gwl isolated from mitotic cells at S90 and S453.
source: Indeed, purified active Fcp1 (Fcp1WT), but not an inactive, catalytic dead, Fcp1 version (Fcp1CD), was able to dephosphorylate Gwl isolated from mitotic cells at both sites (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro phosphatase assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Pre-treatment of mitotic Gwl with Fcp1WT, but not with Fcp1CD, substantially reduced Gwl ability to phosphorylate S67-Ensa.
source: The results clearly show that pre-treatment of mitotic Gwl with Fcp1WT, but not with Fcp1CD, substantially reduced Gwl ability to phosphorylate S67-Ensa (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: V5-GwlS90A and V5-GwlS453A mutant proteins have significantly reduced S67-Ensa kinase activity compared to V5-GwlWT.
source: assaying S67-Ensa kinase activity of V5-GwlS90A and V5-GwlS453A mutant proteins, isolated from transfected and prometaphase-arrested HeLa cells, revealed that both mutants had significantly reduced S67-Ensa kinase activity compared to V5-GwlWT (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The S90A mutation of human Gwl showed highest kinase reduction similarly to what reported for a non-phosphorylatable mutant at equivalent residues in X. laevis Gwl.
source: The S90A mutation of human Gwl showed highest kinase reduction similarly to what reported for a non-phosphorylatable mutant at equivalent residues in X. laevis Gwl (Blake-Hodek et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with cited literature.

claim: A non-phosphorylatable Gwl mutant at S452 (V5-GwlS452A) had S67-Ensa kinase activity similar to GwlWT.
source: Moreover, a non-phosphorylatable Gwl mutant at S452 (V5-GwlS452A), just preceding serine S453, that is not in a Cdk1 phosphorylation consensus but is found phosphorylated in mitotic cells (Dephoure et al., 2008), had S67-Ensa kinase activity similar to GwlWT (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: S452 of Gwl is not in a Cdk1 phosphorylation consensus but is found phosphorylated in mitotic cells.
source: a non-phosphorylatable Gwl mutant at S452 (V5-GwlS452A), just preceding serine S453, that is not in a Cdk1 phosphorylation consensus but is found phosphorylated in mitotic cells (Dephoure et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citation to proteomic data.

claim: Treatment with Cdk1 inhibitor for 15 min completely abolished Gwl activity in control cells but had negligible effects in Fcp1-depleted cells.
source: In addition, we assessed the S67-Ensa kinase activity of Gwl isolated from the same lysates of the experiment described in Figure 2E in which control, Fcp1-depleted and Fcp1-depleted and complemented prometaphase-arrested cells were treated with the Cdk1 inhibitor for 15 min, and found that while this treatment completely abolished Gwl activity in control cells it had negligible effects in Fcp1-depleted cells (Figure 4C; see also Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Prolonging Cdk1 inhibitor treatment up to 30 min resulted in a reduction of Ensa kinase activity of Gwl also in Fcp1-depleted cells.
source: Like for Gwl dephosphorylation, prolonging Cdk1 inhibitor treatment up to 30 min resulted in a reduction of Ensa kinase activity of Gwl also in Fcp1-depleted cells
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The 15-min treatment with RO-3306 induced full pT320-PP1cα dephosphorylation in Fcp1-depleted cells without significantly affecting Gwl kinase activity towards Ensa.
source: Nevertheless, it is important to remark that the 15-mintreatment with RO-3306 induced full pT320-PP1cα dephosphorylation in Fcp1-depleted cells without significantly affecting Gwl kinase activity towards Ensa (Figures 2E and 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2E and 4C.

claim: By controlling Cdk1 and Gwl inactivation, Fcp1 appears to be at the apex of a phosphorylation cascade required to exit mitosis.
